title: “Evil Mickey Mouse” Invades Japan in a 1934 Japanese Anime Propaganda Film
description:
in Film |   	September 11th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Before the Japan­ese fell com­plete­ly, one hun­dred per­cent in love with any­thing an
body:
in Film |   	September 11th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Before the Japan­ese fell com­plete­ly, one hun­dred per­cent in love with any­thing and every­thing Dis­ney (I mean, seri­ous­ly, they love it), Mick­ey Mouse rep­re­sent­ed some­thing com­plete­ly dif­fer­ent: Pure Amer­i­can impe­ri­al­ist evil.
At least he did in this 1934 ani­mat­ed pro­pa­gan­da car­toon Omochabako series dai san wa: Ehon senkya-hyaku­san­ja-rokunen (Toy­box Series 3: Pic­ture Book 1936) by Komat­suza­wa Hajime. It’s a con­vo­lut­ed title, but pret­ty sim­ple in plot. An island of cute crit­ters (includ­ing one Felix the Cat clone) is attacked from the air by an army of Mick­ey Mous­es (Mick­ey Mice?) rid­ing bats and assist­ed by croc­o­diles and snakes that act like machine guns. The fright­ened crea­tures call on the heroes of Japan­ese sto­ry­books and folk leg­ends to help them, from Momo­taro (“Peach Boy”) and Kin­taro (“Gold­en Boy”) to Issun-boshi (“One Inch Boy”) and Benkei, a war­rior monk, to send Mick­ey pack­ing. The not-so-sub­tle mes­sage: Mick­ey Mouse may be your hero, Amer­i­ca, but our char­ac­ters are old­er, more numer­ous, and way more beloved. Our pop cul­ture is old­er than yours!
Though made in 1934, it is set in 1936, which might tie (accord­ing to this site) into the expi­ra­tion of a naval treaty between the Unit­ed States and Japan on that date. The Japan­ese attack on Pearl Har­bor was a full sev­en years off, but clear­ly ten­sions were run­ning high even then, as both the West and Japan had their eyes on Asia and the South Pacif­ic.
Also of note is the trope of char­ac­ters com­ing alive from a sto­ry­book, as this was a favorite sub­ject in sev­er­al Warn­er Bros. car­toons that would come out a few years lat­er (and which we’ve cov­ered).
And final­ly to clar­i­fy Mickey’s fate at the end of the film: the old man with the box is a Rip Van Win­kle char­ac­ter, and in Japan­ese folk­lore he is made old by the con­tents of a box he’s been told not to open. Vio­lence is not van­quished with vio­lence at the end of this car­toon, but with mag­ic and deri­sive laugh­ter fol­lowed by a song. In the real world, things would not end so eas­i­ly.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.
Relat­ed Con­tent:
Don­ald Duck’s Bad Nazi Dream and Four Oth­er Dis­ney Pro­pa­gan­da Car­toons from World War II
Dr. Seuss’ World War II Pro­pa­gan­da Films: Your Job in Ger­many (1945) and Our Job in Japan (1946)
“The Duck­ta­tors”: Looney Tunes Turns Ani­ma­tion into Wartime Pro­pa­gan­da (1942)
 Ted Mills is a free­lance writer on the arts.

title: Scientists Discover the Earliest Evidence of Drug Use in 25,000-Year-Old Teeth
description:
in Food & Drink, History, Psychology |   	September 11th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image by Fakhri
“Sci­en­tists Dis­cov­er the Ear­li­est Evi­de
body:
in Food & Drink, History, Psychology |   	September 11th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image by Fakhri
“Sci­en­tists Dis­cov­er the Ear­li­est Evi­dence of Drug Use in Real­ly Old Teeth” may sound like odd head­line lan­guage, at least by the tra­di­tion­al stan­dards of the New York Times. But then, the teeth in ques­tion are, indeed, real­ly old. “Archae­ol­o­gists have pushed the time­line of human drug use back fur­ther than ever before by study­ing teeth that belonged to a hunter-gath­er­er who lived in Indone­sia some­time from 16,000 to 25,000 years ago,” writes reporter Becky Fer­reira. This beats the 13,000-year-old beer from Israel that pre­vi­ous­ly held the title of old­est known mind-alter­ing comestible. “The individual’s molars, which were found in a cave on the island of Sulawe­si, are marked with deep grooves that were most like­ly left by inces­sant suck­ing on betel nuts, which release psy­choac­tive stim­u­lants.”
All these mil­len­nia lat­er, betel nut-chew­ing remains a major rit­u­al and pas­time. Though it seems nev­er to have caught on in the Eng­lish-speak­ing world, it has a great many adher­ents in not just mod­ern-day Indone­sia but also oth­er parts of south­east and south Asia, includ­ing India, as well as in Chi­na. 
Mixed into a com­pound with the leaves of its own plant, slaked lime, and a vari­ety of oth­er ingre­di­ents from coconut to men­thol to cloves to tobac­co — the region­al vari­a­tions are count­less — betel nuts can be chewed all day long, and often are. Whether you call it paan, buai, doma, ngangà, or some­thing else entire­ly, the stuff is “reput­ed to be the world’s fourth most pop­u­lar psy­choac­tive sub­stance after alco­hol, caf­feine, and nico­tine,” write the authors of a study on the Sulawe­si teeth new­ly pub­lished in Sci­ence Advances.
Before you seek out the near­est are­ca palm to expe­ri­ence what all the fuss is about for your­self, know that the doc­u­ment­ed health effects of betel nut-chew­ing include can­cer, car­dio­vas­cu­lar dis­ease, liv­er dam­age, dia­betes, and infer­til­i­ty; even still-fer­tile chew­ers run the risk of caus­ing birth defects. At the very least, those who pick up the habit also acquire a char­ac­ter­is­tic red tooth stain, which has been seen on near­ly 5,000-year-old skele­tons unearthed in south­east Asia. In the case of the skull from Sulawe­si, it was­n’t the col­or of the teeth but their wear pat­terns that told the tale. Grif­fith Uni­ver­si­ty pro­fes­sor Adam Brumm, who led the study, hypoth­e­sizes a “neg­a­tive feed­back loop” in which betel nuts inflict­ed den­tal dam­age on these ancient peo­ples, but also offered the only means of reliev­ing the pain of that dam­age. Whether now or 25,000 years ago, if one sub­stance seems to be both caus­ing your prob­lems and pro­vid­ing their solu­tions, it’s prob­a­bly time to quit.
Relat­ed Con­tent:
Humans First Start­ed Enjoy­ing Cannabis in Chi­na Cir­ca 2800 BC
Sci­en­tists Dis­cov­er that Ancient Egyp­tians Drank Hal­lu­cino­genic Cock­tails from 2,300 Year-Old Mug
The Drugs Used by the Ancient Greeks and Romans
The Romans Stashed Hal­lu­cino­genic Seeds in a Vial Made From an Ani­mal Bone
Did Psy­che­del­ic Mush­rooms Appear in Medieval Chris­t­ian Art?: A Video Essay
Hofmann’s Potion: 2002 Doc­u­men­tary Revis­its the His­to­ry of LSD
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Sara Anstis' Soft Pastels Summon Mythology, Dreams, and the Renaissance
description: A figure appears to have been subsumed by a bookcase, and another is swathed in a green sleeping bag beneath a makeshift tent. Whether navigating
body:
A figure appears to have been subsumed by a bookcase, and another is swathed in a green sleeping bag beneath a makeshift tent. Whether navigating a bathtub fitted with oars or sleeping in a bed while stacked like pancakes, the figures in Sara Anstis’ atmospheric drawings are immersed in curious activities. Hints of mysterious narratives, nursery rhymes, art historical iconography, and ancient symbolism make their way into enchanting and peculiar tableaux.
Anstis conjures a timeless air in the small-scale works of her solo show Pastels at Olney Gleason. Over the past couple of years, her palette has shifted to more muted, autumnal tones in contrast to her earlier works that featured vibrant, saturated hues and an almost glowing, neon quality. Recently, she’s looked to art history, particularly medieval and early Renaissance works.
“Ermine” (2026), pastel on paper, 13 3/8 x 18 1/8 inches
The stoic, three-quarter profiles of figure in “The Horse Rider,” for example, reflects expressions seen in the 15th-century work of the likes of Fra Angelico and Hans Memling. “The Painter” ties in the medieval art tradition of placing saints at the foot of a holy figure, this time depicted as women peering reverently not only toward a female artist but the empowering drawn likeness of a woman’s form.
Another recurring animal motif we closely associate with Leonardo da Vinci and his masterpiece “Lady with an Ermine.” For Anstis, these tributes are small in scale but rich in the recognition of women with a variety of talents and interests, not the least of which include motherhood.
The maternal theme emerges in works throughout the exhibition, influenced partly by German artist Paula Modersohn-Becker’s 1906 painting “Self-Portrait at 6th Wedding Anniversary.” Soft pastels are a symbolic and practical medium, building compositions that explore the fuzziness of dreams and the blurred edges of folk stories. “Three heads in a bed,” for example, brings to mind the nursery rhyme “Ten in the Bed,” which is sometimes sung as “Three in the Bed.” 
Long interested in mythology and subjectivity, Anstis renders figures and symbolic objects amid surreal settings. Some works adhere more closely to the conventions of portraiture while others reveal an array of enigmatic, narrative elements. Two disembodied arms hold a small dog around a woman’s shoulders in “The Milkman,” for instance, and a pensive woman walks by a display of numerous tiny vials in “Lachrymatories,” which in ancient Greece and Rome were used to hold perfumes but were once thought to collect mourners’ tears, earning them the name “tear bottles.”
“The Painter” (2026), pastel on paper, 9 7/8 x 8 1/4 inches
Through the use of pastels, Anstis retains “an intimate sense of touch that charges her scenes with introspective intensity,” the gallery says. The women in her works fully embody their surroundings, both emotionally and physically connecting to their activities, be it horseback riding, reading, or painting. Throughout, she evokes an air of veneration, as if to every scene there is some underlying rite or observance of which we’re only seeing a fragment. The artist tips her hat to the absurd, even the slightly cartoonish, tapping into the seductive irrationality of dreams and the imagination.
Pastels is on view through October 24 in New York City. See more on the artist’s Instagram.

title: Symmetry and Biomorphic Forms Characterize Roberta Gentry's Sensual Paintings
description: Through brilliant oranges and moody shades of blue, Los Angeles-based artist Roberta Gentry renders vivid, balanced compositions that, as she says
body:
Through brilliant oranges and moody shades of blue, Los Angeles-based artist Roberta Gentry renders vivid, balanced compositions that, as she says, take the senses seriously. Gentry has long been interested in the relationship between the constructed and the natural, cultivating abstract, biomorphic forms scaffolded by tall columns. 
Gravitating toward symmetry and restricted palettes, Gentry paints rhythmic pieces that adhere to an underlying grid. Every painting is the result of multiple layers of thinned acrylic, which build into subtle gradients that dissipate across the canvas.
“The Rose Lattice” (2026), acrylic on canvas, 36 x 48 inches
The paintings shown here are part of that artist’s upcoming solo exhibition, Blood Orange. Lush with color and texture, Gentry’s pieces reference the 16th-century La Dame à la licorne tapestries, comprised of six fiber works featuring a blond, lavishly dressed noblewoman flanked by a unicorn on one side and a lion on the other. Each piece correlates with one of the five senses, with text on the sixth reading “À Mon Seul Désirm,” or “to my only desire.”
While Blood Orange references the tapestries’ bold color palettes, Gentry also renders various elements they depict. The velvet gown the noblewoman wears, a towering pipe organ, and the orange trees anchoring the backdrop become central forms. 
Although scholars interpret the tapestries as directly referencing the sense, others take a broader, more nuanced approached. The latter posit that the fiber works speak to how we gather knowledge and information about the world—particularly through the sixth, more mysterious piece related to emotion—and this is another place where Gentry’s interests align. She often considers “how we construct mythologies to interpret and explain our lived experiences,” that emerges on the canvas through a tension between the order of the grid and the roving, unpredictable nature of organic growth. 
Blood Orange runs through October 24 at Track 16’s East Hollywood location. Find more from the artist on Instagram.

description:
All images courtesy of TADEO Co., Ltd., shared with permission
September 11, 2026


Have you ever imagined a pear or an apple with a personality? If
body:
All images courtesy of TADEO Co., Ltd., shared with permission
September 11, 2026


Have you ever imagined a pear or an apple with a personality? If the fruit suddenly had two eyes and a stem-like nose, it might look a little like PÉPET, the palm-size “paper friend” produced by TAKEO Co., Ltd. Originally designed by Masae Nagao, the colorful characters come with names like “Dandel,” “Fuji,” and “Sky.” They’re each composed of more than 400 of layers of colorful paper, and they adorably wobble and ruffle when handled.
Inspired by the saturated red and green of apples and their leaves, TAKEO will release a new edition named “Pomme” on October 14. Follow updates on the company’s Instagram.

title: Standing in the Shadow of No Towers
description:
Opinion
                The struggle for immigrant rights and lives after 9/11 defined a generation of South Asian art and activ
body:
Opinion
                The struggle for immigrant rights and lives after 9/11 defined a generation of South Asian art and activism, even if it felt at times like we were trying to empty the ocean with a teaspoon.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Still of Naeem Mohaiemen in Visible Collective, "Disappeared in America: Lingering Twenty" (2004), video (all images courtesy Naeem Mohaiemen, unles otherwise noted)
    
        
            By August, the Tribeca nightclub Vinyl had gone into a Peter Gatien-era meltdown. Time magazine ran a dramatic cover story the year prior (“What Ecstasy Does to Your Brain”) and the dancefloor had posters warning about plainclothes sting ops. There was still talcum powder on the floor for dancing, but euphoric substances had vanished. In all my Sundays of dancing at Vinyl, I had never thought of how close it was to the Twin Towers — until that Tuesday in September when, by nightfall, the pavement outside was stacked with plastic bags of socks, t-shirts, and sweatpants we had collected for tower survivors who were expected to be pulled out “any moment now.” We waited until midnight, and by then it was clear — no one got out alive.HBO Television, where I worked at the time, had a satellite office downtown. When I came out of the subway at Broadway-Lafayette, Amin Miah, the corner fruitseller who usually gave me the “best” banana, started saying in a frenzy, “Duita biman marse, ami dekhsi” (“two planes hit, I saw it” in Bangla). I spoke to him for a moment, looked down Broadway at the smoke plumes, and started walking to the office. It was 9:15am, I knew I was late for the staff meeting preparation, and most people on the street were also trying to get to work. I called Zahed Amanullah, co-editor of Altmuslim, because I figured that as a Berkeley resident, he may not know the news yet. His cellphone went to voicemail; later I learned he was in Cuba visiting José Marti’s grave when the tour guide said, “Something terrible — el cataclismo — has happened, we have to get back to the hotel.”HBO’s Interactive Ventures head, Kevin Dowdell, did his best to pass on a semblance of “normal.” He insisted the staff meeting would start on time, at 10am. Then the South Tower collapsed. We watched it through the window, and then everything started happening in slow motion. Everyone was trying to call family, school, and of course all the phone lines were jammed shut (later we learned the shutdown was actually protocol to keep lines free for emergency communication). My girlfriend at the time, artist Reiko Yamamoto, had no cell phone — most people didn’t, it was still 2001 — and I had no way to reach her, so I biked down to Tribeca to find her. As crowds of businesspeople ran up the street, covered in a white powder, I wondered why nobody was stopping me. Nobody knows what to do anymore, I thought. I arrived at Chambers Street and of course the office had been evacuated already — Tribeca was in the blast radius of the towers, so residents had the sense to shut offices and leave. It was another four hours before Reiko made it home. The first thing I said to her was, “Please, you have to get a cell phone.” It’s likely a lot of people got over their aversion to the still-novel device that day.The next week, I met comrades from South Asian activist organizations Youth Solidarity Summer (YSS) and Taxi Workers Alliance (TWA) outside a vigil. This was organized by Sreenath Sreenivasan of South Asian Journalists Association (SAJA) for a Sikh man who had been a victim of a hate-crime attack in the hours after 9/11. I had a tiny American flag attached to my bike handlebars. Filmmaker Dina Hossain had just finished work on a documentary about Leonard Bernstein for PBS and had started work on a new project on Islam in the world. The timing was absolutely eerie and she was hyper-aware of the loop of history.“Where did you get that flag?” she asked.“Somebody gave it to me, we are all mourning together,” I replied. Dina paused, looked at me, and said, “You will understand that you and I are not going to be allowed to be part of that ‘we,’ not anymore.”Visible Collective, "Disappeared in America: Fear of Flying" (2005), videoSome had longer memories. My cousin Hassan remembered being attacked in 1979 in California as an “Eye-ranian” as the hostage crisis dragged out. Poet Saba Waheed, who had met us at the Vinyl club 9/11 relief point, went home and wrote “when they started bombing…” — memories of the first Gulf War. She ended with “oh no, not again.” I thought she was being extreme. People were in shock, but why would they “nuke Eye-raq”? It took a few days for us to learn that there had been several Bangladeshi waiters working at the Windows on the World restaurant in the first tower. In the citadel of capital, theirs were among the many working-class deaths. The media asked for names, biographies, photos. I understood, at that moment, that “Bangladeshi” had been interpellated as “Muslim.” Those stories of Muslim victims of 9/11 became suddenly essential as the beatings of taxi drivers and shop owners continued. In response, we built up the all-American narrative of model minorities. When scholar Mahmood Mamdani published Good Muslim, Bad Muslim: America, the Cold War, and the Roots of Terror three years later, I had the shock of recognition; I too had been one of those apologetic, get-along-go-along Muslims. We naively thought if we were polite in the face of Islamophobia, it would wilt. Our generation’s approach was to appeal to those in power — to ask, “allow us to go about life in peace.” Thankfully, Mamdani’s son, Zohran, had other ideas. Instead of appealing to the power structure, he worked his way up to being in a position to change the system itself.I lived in Hell’s Kitchen and was sufficiently freaked out by the idea of “another attack” to want to move out of Manhattan. The landlord was thrilled at the chance to raise the rent. He returned my deposit with alacrity. The Russian bouncer at the strip club next door looked at my moving truck and waved at me. He had a scar down his right eye and had “seen it all.” I wondered if he was a veteran of the Chechen wars. On the drive to the Brooklyn storage space, I thought of the magazine profiles that talked about presidents finding God. Surely God was merciful; all the Abrahamic faiths made the same claim. HBO had sponsored my green card application, and the card arrived in the mail in April 2001. It was an innocuous white envelope, and at first I thought it was a credit card offer from Burlington, Vermont. When I realized what it was, I called my immigration lawyer and asked if I could freely go to protests now (the Abner Louima and Amadou Diallo cases had thrown New York into a turmoil of protests against the police).My Oberlin College roommate, Saif, was not so lucky. His green card due date was the end of the year. After September 2001, all such applications were ensnared in the dreaded loop of the security check. Saif had the bad luck of having an extremely common Muslim-Bangladeshi surname. You can imagine how that security check went. His H-1B visa timing ran out, and he returned to Bangladesh to work in the business sector. In a way, many countries benefited from this “reverse brain drain” as many immigrants got fed up with these visa mazes and returned home. Working-class migrants did not have those options, and large extended networks back home often depended on the money they sent back. So by and large they stayed, despite the mass arrests on Coney Island Avenue, or crossed into Canada.

title: University of Michigan’s Fully Funded MFA Program Combines Studio Art and Research
description:
Announcement
                Top-ranked, tuition-free MFA program at University of Michigan's Stamps School of Art & Design supports
body:
Announcement
                Top-ranked, tuition-free MFA program at University of Michigan's Stamps School of Art & Design supports interdisciplinary, research-based practices  
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Crossways, Fiona Hoffer (MFA ’26), MFA Thesis Exhibition. Photo by Andy Maticorena Kajie
    
        
            The University of Michigan’s Penny W. Stamps School of Art & Design, ranked #11 nationally among graduate art and design schools by U.S. News and World Report, is now accepting MFA in Art applications for Fall 2027. The Stamps MFA brings students a uniquely supportive, critically engaged environment for interdisciplinary and research-based creative practice. Led by MFA Program Director Angela Washko, students develop materially sophisticated, conceptually rigorous work informed by funded travel and engagement with diverse communities, institutions, and creative contexts. Graduates emerge prepared to exhibit internationally, secure tenure-track positions at leading institutions, create public art, and shape cultural organizations worldwide.Throughout the two-year program, students engage with faculty from Stamps and tap into the boundless resources and collaborative opportunities that can only be found at the University of Michigan, TIME’s top public research university. Students also connect with nationally and internationally recognized visiting artists and critics through studio visits, critiques, and other events, gaining personalized feedback, fresh perspectives, and valuable professional connections.“I’ve been to a lot of MFA thesis shows around the country and I can say with confidence this is one of the best I’ve encountered — not only because of the strength and complexity and pleasures offered by the individual projects, but also because of the sense that the artists were talking and thinking together, learning and being inspired by each other. That such a strong sense of conversation could result in really unique and individual artistic voices is truly remarkable.”— Aruna D'Souza, Writer and Art CriticVisit the Stamps website to explore the Stamps MFA program through work from our most recent thesis exhibition, and to learn more about our graduate program in our upcoming events, including our Virtual Open House on Thursday, November 12, 2026.
